subject: Chemistry
title: Why Leaves Change Color in Fall
description: A micro-lesson that makes Why Leaves Change Color in Fall usable.

hook.text: The reds and yellows of autumn were hiding in the leaves all summer, masked by green chlorophyll.

buildup.text: Chlorophyll absorbs red and blue light, reflecting green. It dominates while the tree is photosynthesizing.

discovery.text: In fall, trees stop making chlorophyll. As green fades, yellow carotenoids and orange xanthophylls are revealed.

twist.text: Red and purple come from anthocyanins—new pigments made in fall as a sunscreen to protect the dying leaf.

climax.text: Eventually all pigments break down. The leaf turns brown from tannins—and falls.

punchline.text: Green fades, hidden colors emerge, new reds appear. Fall is a chemistry show.

quiz.question: Where do the yellow and orange fall colors come from?
options: Carotenoid pigments that were hidden by green chlorophyll all summer
New pigments produced as the leaf dies
Sunlight reflecting differently off dry leaves

details.summary: Leaves change color in autumn because trees stop producing green chlorophyll as daylight decreases, revealing yellow and orange carotenoid pigments that were always present. Red and purple colors come from anthocyanins, newly synthesized compounds that may protect leaves during nutrient recovery.
details.whyItMatters: Autumn leaf chemistry illustrates pigment biochemistry, photoprotection, and seasonal plant metabolism. It demonstrates how multiple chemical systems within a single cell create visible color changes.
takeaways: Green chlorophyll breaks down first, revealing hidden carotenoids
Anthocyanins are produced fresh in autumn and create red hues
Shorter days trigger the chemical process, not cooler temperatures

faq.question: Why do some trees turn red while others turn yellow in fall?
faq.answer: Yellow trees primarily reveal carotenoid pigments already present beneath the chlorophyll. Red trees actively produce anthocyanins, a process that requires sugars and light. Species like maples produce abundant anthocyanins while oaks and birches typically rely on carotenoid yellows and browns.

faq.question: Do autumn leaf colors serve any biological purpose for the tree?
faq.answer: The anthocyanins producing red color may act as sunscreen, protecting leaf cells while the tree reabsorbs valuable nitrogen from chlorophyll. By shielding the photosynthetic machinery from excess light during breakdown, the tree recovers more nutrients before the leaves drop.
